speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend call an all-night sitting and three previous occasions when the appropriation was before the House, a "few hours"? If all the hours were put together, I am sure they would comprise something like two days;

For a scheme like that, it was a very few hours to discuss the policy of the Government, and the time was so short that even now we have not the necessary information. The attitude of the Government was the application of arbitrary methods that the people of this country cannot and will not tolerate for very long. It was a violation of the fundamental principles of responsible Government. It was the application of the' autocratic rules which existed before the Magna Charta, when constitutional Government was unknown, when the people had no right to be heard and when the only governmental principle was "taxation without representation." Perhaps this is a digression; but let me say that the first thing that we should preserve in this country above any matter, (financial or economic, is -responsible Government. We shall not forget the struggles that the people had to go through before being

recognized, before obtaining the consecration of the principle that their representatives should have absolute control of all moneys asked for and spent by the Government. For my part, I diaim that this principle has been wilfully and generally ignored and violated by this Administration, and that the tendencies of this Government have been such in that respect that the main issue during the next general election should be the necessity of re-establishment of responsible Government in Canada. This will be the best kind of reconstruction work for our country. It will furnish the best contribution to its greatness and prosperity, and to the welfare and happiness of its people.
May I also be permitted to say that amongst the many problems that we have to face in Canada, there is one of importance that should not be overlooked, and that is the question of the relations between capital and labour. Generally speaking, the workers throughout Canada are not satisfied with existing conditions; there is a certain amount of discontent and unrest.
. To that condition of affairs many causes may have contributed, which it would be too long and too difficult to analyse because they pertain to the social, psychological and economic domains. But I think we can arrive at this conclusion, that labour will never revert to its pre-war condition. For myself, I am glad of that, because I do firmly believe that in the past the workers all over the world did not get a fair share of the happiness and good things of life. I am a believer in the principle of fraternity and equality; I think it is only by the application of this Christian principle that our civilization can be saved. I believe it is the duty of every public man to give this question of the relations between capital and labour his best attention in order to find some way of effecting a reconciliation between these two elements. If the House will permit me, I will give my own personal opinion as to the ways and means that might be adopted to attain such a result.
There are, according to my mind, two ways by which a reconciliation can be effected. First, the workers should be satisfied that they are getting a reasonable share of the profits realized from their work. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, I do not say that they should have an equal share of the profits. What is in my mind is this: that they should have a reasonable participation in the profits, after allowance
218J
has been made for the risks and responsibility of the employers, for the costs of materials, administration, and executive, for running and overhead charges, and manufacturer's profit. Or Sir, excess profits should be employed to form a reserve fund to provide for old age pensions, mother's and widow's pensions or other humanitarian institutions. I think |we should always remember that labour is a living, fighting force, fighting for equality, and that it will not stop until it achieves a victory.
Coming back to the question of the necessity for economy, as I said before, I cannot see any evidence of any such spirit in the policy of the Government. I have spoken of the railway and shipbuilding policies of the Government, which, to my mind, are nothing but a negation of any principle of economy. Let me now point to some other matters that call for the immediate attention of the Canadian Government, if we are ever to get out of our difficulties. There is for instance, the question of the Civil Service. For my part, I believe that our Civil Service is inadequate in this sense, that we have by far too many civil servants. I think that their number should be gradually reduced. I believe that some millions of dollars could be saved in that direction, and I think that that is a work that should be started at once.
There is another question upon which I desire to say a few words, and that is the question of military expenditure. The Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) quoted some statistics the other day going to show that Canada's expenditure on naval and military defence was lower than that of any other country in the world. Sir, we know that comparisons are odious, and this case, I think, is no exception to the rule. To compare Canada with sovereign countries seems to me to be no more reasonable than to compare the physical strength of a man with that of a child; and when you compare Canada with the other Dominions, if you wish to make a. fair comparison, there are many things that you must take into consideration. First of all, we should look not merely at the amount expended in only one branch of the administration of a country, but at the total expenditure of every one of these Dominions with which a comparison is made. Their geographical situation must also be taken into account, as well as other factors. But even if all these conditions were exactly the same in the different countries that my hon. friend the minister has mentioned, I

do not think we can fairly conclude that because one country is spending too much money in one direction, we should also do the same thing. If the minister is satisfied with his statistics, I certainly believe that the people of this country do not share his satisfaction. For my part, in view of the very grave financial situation of Canada, and of the additional taxation to be imposed, I was expecting a substantial reduction in our military expenditure. The expenditure of $12,000,000 for military purposes is, in my opinion, nothing short of extravagance, and the same can be said of many public works such, for instance, as: the Victoria dry dock, which is the subject of some interesting discussion at the present moment; the Toronto harbour; the St. John harbour; improvements to the Welland and Trent canals; and other undertakings of that character. In the face of these extravagances it is nothing but provocation to the people for the Government now to talk about additional taxation. As I said, economy should be the watchword everywhere, and it is for this Government to set the example.
There is one matter of supreme importance, in regard to which the Government will have to render strict account, and that is the acceptance of the battleships offered by the Admiralty. The attitude of the Government in this matter had no justification whatever. We should not spend one cent on the expansion of the Canadian navy. Sir, we have nothing to fear, and, therefore, we do not need a navy. There is only one country with whom we might expect to have difficulties, and that is, our neighbours to the south of us, the United States. I am sure, however, that there is no hon. member in this House who would say that there is, or can be, any reasonable fear of such a calamity as a rupture between us and the United States. It would be absurd and entirely wrong on our part to provoke any serious conflict with them, and it would be equally unjustifiable and unjust for them to do anything that would incur our enmity. All that we need in the way of a Canadian naval force is a fleet that will provide protection for our fisheries, protection not against any nation, but against individuals. I say that the acceptance of these battleships will simply burden the people of this country with a very large and unnecessary expenditure for which there can be no excuse, and I therefore register my protest against such a policy. Some one will probably say that we on this side of the House did once favour a
I Mr. Demers.]
Canadian navy. I shall not pay any more attention to that question than to say that we submited our policy to the people and it was rejected. Is there any reason to believe that the public sentiment in that respect has changed, especially when there is no longer ground for the fear that existed then, and when the causes for apprehension have disappeared? There is something more to say on this question. These battleships were accepted without the consent of the people or of Parliament, and the consequences of this action may prove of very great national importance. The acceptance of a gift of such a nature may well involve dangerous obligations in the future, and I cannot too strongly express my protest against the autocratic and unconstitutional action of the Government in this matter.
I said a moment ago that economy is absolutely necessary everywhere to-day; but economy, Mr. Speaker, is not the only necessity in Canada. There is one great principle, the application of which will do more than anything else to accomplish the great work of reconstruction which rests with the public men of this country. That principle is this: Mind your own business. That principle is that Canada should be the only object of our attention and consideration at this time. We should restrict our activities to Canada exclusively. Our country is large enough to require the concentration of all our energies towards its development. Let us be Canadians first, [DOT]and Canadians only; let us get out of European and Imperial affairs. It is about time that the true Canadian began the work of creating an exclusive Canadian sentiment in this country, and there could be no better time than now that we realize that we cannot ever meet its requirements.
I was impressed the other day with an article which I read in no less important a paper than the Montreal Gazette, which declared that Parliament is sick of the League of Nations and of trips to Europe by Cabinet ministers. I thought that that was the real feeling of a good many members of this House, also, if they would only voice it. At any rate, any man who does not agree with that view must admit that he has not learned the lessons of true Cana-dianism which we received from the two great leaders, Macdonald and Laurier.
Sir, Canada is the only country in the world for us; it is all that we can call our own, and it is so immense in area and of such vast possibilities that it will take all our time to develop it. Let us not only

sing, but let us feel and fully appreciate the sentiment of our national anthem, "0! Canada."
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to deal with any other questions at this time, but before resuming my seat, I should like to summarize, in a few words, my views as to the methods which this Government should adopt to carry out the work of reorganization and reconstruction: First, an exclusively Canadian policy; second, restoration of responsible government; third, solution of labour problems; and, fourth, economy in every branch of administration. Such is, Sir, to my mind, the policy that would restore prosperity and greatness to Canada. 1
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton, N.B.): Mr. Speaker, I have followed with a great deal of interest the different speeches that have been delivered during this debate. I must say, however, that I was rather disappointed in the speech the Prime Minister delivered on Friday last. I think the members of this House, and the people of the country, expected the Prime Minister to deal with the very serious problems that face the country to-day-the railway situation, the unemployment situation, and the other serious issues that confront the country. But what were we treated to on the part of the right hon. gentleman? He gave one of the greatest expositions of ridicule and abuse that this House has ever witnessed. The Prime Minister accused our little group, in this part of the chamber, of not moving their platform in Parliament. Mr. Speaker, it reminds me of a passage in a book that hon. gentlemen are more or less familiar with: Cast not your pearls before swine.
Oh, oh.

We have moved this platform before a tribunal that is possibly less prejudiced than this House, a tribunal higher than Parliament itself-the electors of Canada. That platform has been endorsed in a large number of cases where it was tried out before the people on its merits, and if it is endorsed to as great an extent at the next general election as it has been in the recent by-elections we will have no cause to complain.
I think it was very small politics for the Prime Minister to try to make out that we were an "annex" to the Liberal party simply because we propose to vote for the amendment before the House, in view of the fact that we have supported the
Government with our votes in this House nearly as often as we have opposed them. As to where we stand I think, Mr. Speaker, I cannot do better than quote what I said last year on the Budget because what I said at that time is quite applicable to our position to-day. Speaking on May 27, 1920, I expressed myself as follows:
-we do not propose to support either of the old parties in this House. When a question arises such as the present question before the House we intend to take a stand on it that will be in the best interests of Canada. We may err, but if we do we shall err in judgment; we shall not be whipped into line to support this party or that against our convictions,-do not make any mistake about that. I think that we have proved our independence in this House during the present session; we have voted with the Government perhaps as often as against them. I am only sorry that we were not able to vote with them oftener, because if we had been able to vote with them it would have meant that they were bringing down good legislation, legislation for the good of Canada and which we would have been pleased to support.
I do not wish to take up a great deal of time in this debate, because the discussion has run at some length now, and after matters of this kind have been discussed for three or four days there is not very much new left to be said with respect to them. I do, however, wish to give a concrete example or two of how a protective tariff affects the business of the country, and how extravagant a method it is of collecting a revenue, and I wish to take in illustration some articles I know something about-articles that are used in my own province very largely.
For one thing I wish to speak of the duty on fertilizers. At the present time, as you all know, there is a duty of 10 per cent on mixed fertilizer, whilst chemicals, with the exception of acid phosphates, are admitted to the country free. I have here the imports of fertilizers for the last ten years, giving the amount imported that was dutiable and the amount imported that was free. Some of the recent speakers have referred to the Canadian tariff as inducing American manufacturers to locate in Canada. I want to show you why that is the case-because while they are able to import into Canada their raw materials free they are able to charge a duty on the manufactured article, collect it from the people of Canada and put it into their pockets instead of that duty going into the revenues of the' country. For instance, in 1912 we imported $413,338 worth of fertilizers that were dutiable, and on those imports collected $41,333 in duty.

That same year there was imported, duty free, fertilizer materials to the value of $735,053.
Had these materials been dutiable the duty collected would have been $73,505. But that went into the manufacturer's pocket, not into the revenue of the country. Therefore, for every dollar that we collected in duty that year the manufacturer put nearly two dollars in his pocket. I do not know that I will trouble the House to give the figures for each year separately. I wish to state, however, that in the ten years we collected in duty on fertilizers imported into Canada $769,585.20, and we imported, duty free, fertilizer materials on which, had there been duty the customs imposed would have amounted to $1,766,134.90. It is just possible that some hon. member will say: Well, the fertilizer manufacturers do not take advantage of this. Very well, I want to disabuse the minds of hon. gentlemen in that particular. I have here the price lists of a firm-an American firm by the way-who have a factory in Canada, a mixing plant. They import their chemicals free of duty and sell the finished product in Canada as well as in the United States. Living as I do only six miles from the American boundary I know whereof I speak In regard to this matter. I have here the lists of this company giving the prices at which they sell in the state of Maine and in the province of New Brunswick. Now, the fertilizers which they sell in Maine for $62.50 they sold in New Brunswick this year for $77.50, a difference of $15 a ton. Yet the chemicals were brought from the same source and it was the same company doing business in both instances. Another fertilizer that they sold in Maine for $67.75, they sold in New Brunswick for $82.75. Another brand, of a higher grade, they sold in Maine for $75.75 and in New Brunswick for $90.75. Owing to this fact our farmers' organizations have taken to buying their own chemicals and importing them themselves. Accordingly this year we were able to lay down at the farmer's local railway station, chemicals such as used in the brand that our dealer charged $77.50 for at $46.18, a difference of $31.32. The farmers, of course, have the remedy in their own hands, and I feel they are going to avail themselves of it- they will simply import their own chemicals and mix their own fertilizers.
I now wish, very briefly, to illustrate how a heavy duty affects our exports. We grow in New Brunswick large quantities of potatoes; that is the reason we use so
[Mr. Caldwell.l
much fertilizer. The latter part of this past season the prices have been very poor in New Brunswick, and we are not realizing a very good price for potatoes at the present time. However, I notice that the potatoes exported during the present year, that is up to the end of March last, have brought a higher average' price than those exported last year when the prices were quoted so high. The high price of last year caused different members to fling the accusation at the farmers that they were profiteers, that they were selling potatoes at $12 a barrel. Potatoes did go to that price in April last year for the simple reason that there were no potatoes in New Brunswick. The potato crop in Canada the past season on the whole, sold at a higher price than the year before. Prices are very low at the present time, for the reason that there is an over-supply on hand and the demand is not equal to the supply. I have here figures of potato exports from Canada to the United States from 1912 to 1921. Of course, during the few war years prices and conditions were abnormal and therefore I shall take two years before the war and two years after and compare them. During the two years before the war there was a duty against our potatoes going to the United States which made the export business rather unprofitable for us. In 1912 we exported 27,286 bushels at a price of 70 cents a bushel; in 1913 152,557 bushels, at a price of 84 cents a bushel; in 1920-when there was no duty-5,480,754 bushels at a price of $1.25 a bushel; and in 1921, 4,204,684 bushels at a price of $1.98 a bushel. It will be noticed that in 1920 we exported over 5,000,000 bushels as compared with only 27,000 bushels in 1912.
When the Fordney Tariff Bill was proposed I took it upon myself to write to the Prime Minister to know if our Government could not take some steps to overcome this Bill. Of course, I realized, as our Prime Minister informed me, that the United States Government have full authority to legislate for themselves, and would resent any interference. At the same time, in view of the fact that Canada has practically a monopoly of the pulp-wood supply of North America, it seemed to me that our Government could very well have put it up to the United States Government that if they discriminated against our farm products it might be necessary for Canada to impose a heavy export duty on pulpwood. I think if this

had been done the United States would have thought twice before passing an Act discriminating against our farm products.
I do not know whether such representations were made or not by our Government to the. Government of the United States, but at any rate this country had had no intimation of any such action having been taken.
In view of the fact that the Young Emergency Tariff measure will affect the potato growers of Eastern Canada very severely, I should like to urge upon the Government the necessity for providing facilities at the port of St. John for the shipping of potatoes during the winter season. If we are practically shut out of the United States, Cuba is our next best market. During the past winter I received several communications from potato shippers in New Brunswick urging me to see if the Government would provide some means for shipping potatoes through the port of St. John during the winter season.
I believe it would not be a costly matter -merely the erection of a frost proof warehouse. These shippers advised me that during last winter they were compelled to ship via Boston, which meant, according to the ruling of the Railway Commission, that they had to pay freight in American funds from the shipping point in Canada to Boston, and from Boston to Cuba. Had they been able to ship by the port of St. John the- difference in the rate of exchange on the freight and in the short rail haul and the longer water haul would have meant practically a dollar a barrel difference in favour of the farmers. I sincerely hope that the Government will take this into consideration and provide the necessary facilities at the port of St. John for handling what is the big export crop from the province of New Brunswick. There are already facilities at the port for handling our western grain, facilities that the whole Dominion has helped to provide, and I think it is no more than fair that the province in which this port is situated should have the facilities required for handling its potatoes.
In speaking of how a high tariff affects imports and exports, I would crave the indulgence of the House while I read an extract from the Montreal Gazette as to what the minority members of the House of Representatives think of the Fordney Tariff Bill.
In the minority report the Republicans are accused of tossing into the lap of "three great trusts, the packers, the sugar trust and the -woollen trusts $775,000,000 a year," and of seeking to disbar any future trade with the Central Powers and smaller states in Europe through
"a subtle and dangerous joker," in directing the Secretary of the Treasury to fix the value of foreign money as a basis for levying duties on imports.
The present bill is characterized as even worse than its predecessor, the Fordney measure, by the report which asserts that "if any advantage will apply anywhere from the new proposal, it will be to the trusts, speculators and profiteers."
It also calls attention to provisions of the Republican national platform-
By the way, that platform provided for a decrease in the cost of living.
-and inquires whether -any honest 'Republican can sincerely vote for this bill in the belief that it will reduce the oost of living."
"We note that the bill has been changed since the last session of Congress," the report adds, "from the Fordney Emergency Tariff Bill to the Young Emergency Tariff Bill. Whether the ways and means committee throught the name of its chairman, Mr. Fordney, attached to the bill, would discredit it or believed that by attaching the name of Young from the agricultural state of North Dakota, it would more easily fool the farmers, we cannot undertake to say. But there must ibe some political significance in it."
"Figures were presented to show that the actual increase in living costs resulting from enactment of such law would be about $2,000,000,000 a year. The statement says that the bill would hand a gratuity of $125,000,000 annually to the sugar trust $550,000,000 annually to the meat and beef trust, and more than $100,000,000 a year to the income of the woollen trust.
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that a high tariff has that effect in any country. I realize, however, that in view of the Young Emergency Tariff Bill going into effect our Administration will have to be governed in their tariff legislation accordingly, but I hope they will not increase the duty, for instance, on fertilizers, with which we grow potatoes, because we have to pay that import duty, and also the duty on our potatoes going into the United States. Somebody will say: That is not logical; if we pay the duty on the fertilizer coming in, why will we pay the duty on the potatoes going out? The explanation is simply this, that our export trade in potatoes to the United States compared with the quantity of potatoes they grow is a very small factor in fixing the price in that country. For that reason, we being the little fellow, the price is practically set by the big fellow. In that connection, a duty of 25 cents a bushel is being imposed on our potatoes entering the United States, while their potatoes enter Canada free to-day. I think under these circumstances our home market for potatoes should be reserved to Canadian growers. In the next two months we will have a large quantity of potatoes on our hands, and they certainly will not all be disposed of in Eastern Canada, as the new potatoes coming in from the United

States 'will take the place of our own product. Our shippers tell me that if retaliation is proposed by this Government it should be in such a form as will offset the duty that the United States has imposed on articles imported from this country. Of course, you will hear the old cry: Where will you get the revenue from? Well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help thinking that there is as much in the spending of the revenue of the country as there is in collecting it. It seems to me that if our Government had not seen fit to loan $23,000,000 to Roumania in 1919 we would not have needed so much revenue. The very fact of our immense debt makes it clear that Canada had no money to lend, least of all to a bankrupt country from which there is very little prospect of ever getting either the principal or interest. That interest was to have been paid twice a year, but already nearly a million and a half is overdue, and I doubt very much if it ever will be paid. Not only have we thrown this $23,000,000 away; but the people of Canada will have to pay interest on it until the Victory bonds through which we obtained this money to squander are redeemed. I think it would have been a good thing for this country if the revenue in the past few years had not been quite so large; the Government would not have been quite so ready to squander it in loans to bankrupt countries, nor to apply the closure in this House very recently in order to vote $8,0000,000 to build ships for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine at exorbitant prices. If I am not mistaken-the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) will correct me if I am wrong-the price paid for the building of vessels in Canada recently has been $191 a ton. I believe that a firm in Montreal bought a couple of vessels. very recently for somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50 a ton. Of course, we realize that that does not represent the cost of building the vessels, but there are numberless ships idle to-day and no doubt the owners of these were in difficult financial circumstances and were glad to realize money on them at any price. I believe that a member of this firm made the statement that very soon it would be possible to buy ships in Canada at $25 a ton, because large numbers of vessels are at present tied up and unable to get sufficient freight to enable them to pay operating expenses.
I have spoken of the loan to Roumania. At the time it was made we all wondered why the Government was so willing to lend 
money to anybody at that time, to say nothing of lending it to a bankrupt country. The answers to questions put on the Order Paper last year by the member for Chambly-V ercheres (Mr. Archambault) throw some light on why the Government authorized this loan. If I remember rightly the hon. member inquired who were the firms who supplied the goods to Roumania and Greece and what were the prices. It is my memory that the names of a number of firms were given but that the prices were not stated. It was with more or less amazement that members of the House read the answers to those replies, and that they found that a large quantity of goods furnished to Roumania and Greece on this credit or loan was furnished by firms of which supporters of the Government were members, of which some hon. members of this House were presidents and managing directors. If an individual member of Parliament had sold any goods in this way and for this purpose, he would have to resign his seat. But the supporters of the Government were able to get away with it, due to the fact that they were members of these companies. I think, however, we will all admit, that they got very close to the edge.
In dealing with the question where the revenue was to come from I pointed out last year, when speaking on the Budget, a source of revenue that this Government had not only failed to take advantage of but had made it impossible for any succeeding government to take advantage of, namely, Victory bonds exempt from taxation, amounting in all to $1,358,000,000.- More than that, it cost the country nearly $14,000,000 to float those loans, in the payment of commissions to agents who canvassed for the sale of the bonds and to the banks for handling the amounts as they were turned over. We have never been able and never will be able to collect one cent by way of tax on the income derived by the holders of these bonds amounting to $1,358,000,000. I said at the time it was , proposed to make this loan free from taxation that I could hardly find language strong enough to express my disapproval of that course. The Finance Minister pointed out that if the Government did not exempt the bonds from taxation they would not be able to float the loan. Well, it is a fact that the later loan in 1919, which was made taxable, was over-subscribed just as readily as the non-taxable loans; therefore the theory of the Minister of Finance was disproved. Certainly it is harder to sell a

taxable bond, once you set the precedent of not taxing, than to sell a non-taxable bond, but, as I say, the loan in 1919, which was not exempt from taxation, was largely oversubscribed. I have made an estimate of what the income would be by way of income tax if these loans had not been exempt from taxation. The income on $1,358,000,000 at 5J per cent would be $74,690,000. It is fair to suppose that $37,345,000, or half this amount, would be taxable as income at the rate of 4 per cent, because, I think, it is true that these moneys were not all subscribed by the poorer people; it is fair to assume that half the people who subscribed to the loans would have incomes taxable at the rate of 4 per cent. This would add $1,493,800 to the revenue of the country. I think it may be assumed also that the other half of the $74,690,000 would be taxable at the rate of 8 per cent, which would yield a revenue of $2,987,600. I also believe that half of this revenue from interest on Victory bonds would be " received by persons whose incomes were large enough to pay a surtax of 3 per cent, and that would add another $1,120,350 to the revenue of the country, or a total of $5,601,750 yearly. But due to the fact that this tax exemption was made as part of the agreement when the bonds were issued, no government will ever be able to make these bonds taxable which I consider is very unfortunate in view of the fact that we must raise such a very large revenue, a revenue double per capita that raised in the United States. I think it has been stated that the amount which we must raise per capita in order to obtain the necessary revenue will amount to about $70 per capita or $350 for each family of five in this country. The expenditure per capita in the United States is $35 per head, or just half of what ours is. The Secretary of the Treasury of the United States has warned the United States Government that . they must retrench, that the country cannot stand the present extravagant rate of expenditure. When you compare the revenue which they raise per capita with ours, you will see that they spend one dollar per head for every two dollars per head that we spend in Canada. I do rfot think any member of this House, and I am sure that no elector in this country will contend that we are able to pay twice the amount of taxes per head that the citizens of the United States could pay.
I think it was a very unwise thing to abolish the luxury taxes, having regard to the facts concerning our expenditure. The
sound way to raise revenue is by taxing a man on what he is worth, not on what he consumes. The fact that the luxury tax was a good revenue getter was another reason why it should not have been abolished. During the six months that it was in operation it produced somewhere in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000 more than the sales tax has produced in ten months. The luxury tax fell upon people who were better able to pay than the majority of those who will be called upon to contribute to the revenue through the medium of the sales tax which is to take the place of the luxury tax. In my opinion the business profits tax should also have been continued. The people would be interested to know, I am sure, just what was behind the abolition of the luxury tax and the business profits tax, and I propose, before I conclude my remarks, to give them just a little information in regard to this matter.
At Six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, ivhen the House rose at six o'clock, I had just arrived at that point in my remarks where I was saying that I believed that the consuming public of Canada would be anxious to know what influences were behind the Government to induce them to abolish the luxury and business profits taxes which were such good revenue getters. I said that I hoped to be able to enlighten the House and possibly the country as to just what these influences were that induced the Government to do this very unbusinesslike act. I wish to quote from an article that was printed in the Montreal Gazette of May 12, 1920. There were very big headlines on this article: "Million Dollar Fund for Propaganda." Then in somewhat smaller headlines were the words, "Canadian Manufacturers' Association Insistent Upon Tariff Commission of Specialists." The article goes on:
A million dollar fund for the propaganda of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was foreshadowed to night at the annual dinner of the Montreal Branch. Among the guests were Col. W. Grant Morden, Sir James McKechie, head of the Vickers firm.of England and many of thQ business leaders of the province.
T. P. Howard, as President of the Dominion Manufacturers' Association, said that they had approached the Government on the necessity for a scientific tariff board for Canada and stated that it would be considered with the support of

1,600 labor unions of Canada as well as the manufacturers, and in a defence of great industrial mergers both here and in England.
With regard to this demand of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for a scientific tariff board for Canada, I understand that their wish was to have a tariff commission appointed that would deal with the tariff in much the same way that the present Board of Railway Commissioners deals with freight and passenger rates-a board that would have absolute control over what the tariff on all imports should be, and a board that would not be responsible to the electors. I wish to congratulate the Government on withstanding the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in this demand. To appoint such a board would be very unconstitutional, and I am pleased that the Government did not do it. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, not being able to accomplish this object, evidently turned their attention to the matter of outlining a plan of taxation for Canada, for in the Montreal Gazette of a later date, I find the following:
March 29, 1921.-The question of Federal taxation will Ibe discussed here this week by representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, and the Wholesale Merchants' Association, as a result of an intimation from Sir Henry Drayton, Minister of Finance, that he wishes to obtain the collective judgment of the business interests in Canada as to the most desirable plan to raise revenue for Federal requirements.
It is quite evident that these people had raised their million dollar fund, and had assured the Government that they could deliver them the support of 1,600 labour unions. Here we find the Minister of Finance telling them: All right, if you can deliver me this support, get together and tell us what you want, and we will see if we can meet your requirements. I think most people will agree on looking over the Budget that all of the requests made by the big interests of Canada have been granted except one. I believe they wanted in addition to the abolition of the business profits tax and the balance of the luxury taxes, the income tax on corporations abolished. I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance on not acceding to this last request, but it is just possible that he is coming to that by easy stages, and that that tax may be the next thing to go; I hope not, however.
During the war, the slogan in Canada was: The last man and the last dollar. We got the required men all right, but I am sorry to say that the Government did

not begin to get the first dollar of big profits made on war contracts during the war. I think the Government and the Minister of Finance were about two, if not three years too late in starting to tax the excess profits of the business interests of Canada. And I believe it would be unsound to abolish that tax at the present time.
I wish to quote a few extracts from thei Montreal Star of May 12, 1921, which prove conclusively, if proof were needed, that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the other interests allied with them were the instigators of the present taxation scheme for Canada:
"It appears to me that the Finance Minister has worked out the matter in a very clear and concise way," said F. W. iStewart, Chairman of the Montreal Branch of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. "It appears to have been very carefully designed, and the changes made are in the best interests of business. The sales tax is really the basis on which taxation will affect the consumer the least. The manufacturer does not absorb it, and by showing it separately on his invoice no advance is added to it. The sales tax was working very satisfactorily indeed, and its continuation will be satisfactory to wholesalers and manufacturers."
I cannot for the life of me see how Mr. Stewart comes to the conclusion that the sales tax will affect the consumer least, because it is the consumer who pays that tax. Mr. Stewart admits that the wholesaler does not absorb it, so he must pass it on to the consumer. I quote again:
The new budget provisions bring a welcome relief to the ardent card player, to whom the high cost of cards has (been a source of freque.it complaints. The tax on cards not exceeding $24 a gross, is reduced "from 15 cents a pack to 8 cents, and that on cards costing over $24 a gross, drops from 25 cents a pack to 15 cents.
I suppose that the ardent card player, the people who have leisure to indulge in card playing, and the card sharper who fleeces the innocent victim out of his money at cards, will no doubt be benefited by the Budget provisions in this respect, but I do not know whether it is in the best interests of the country or not. I leave that for the House to judge. Another quotation:
The Retail Merchants' Association of Canada is well pleased with the budget, and is glad its work has resulted in what it has been aiming at.	>
So if we needed any further proof that the Budget was the work of the Retail and Wholesale Merchants' Associations and of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, I think we have it here in the avowal that the Retail Merchants' Association have accomplished what they were aiming at. Again:

"So far as we can judge, Sir Henry Drayton has taken the best possible course in his budget," said T. P. Howard, ex-President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and President of the Howard Smith Paper Mills, Ltd. "The abolition of the business profits tax is good. We realize that Sir Henry had to get revenue, and he has done it in the way that presses least heavily on the taxpayer and on business."
When you take out the taxpayer and the business man, who is left to pay the taxes? It is evidently the consumer who owns no property, according to this man, because it is the non-taxpayer, and not the business man. It is the poor labouring man who is working in a mill or on the railroads for $2 or $3 a day, trying to support a large family, who is raising the revenue by paying a tax on everything that he and his family eat and wear. If that is a sound method of taxation, I will admit that I do not know very much about economics. My idea of equitable taxation is to raise the revenue by taxing the men best able to bear it, the men who own property, or who make big profits out of business. It has been said that the reason why the business profits tax was abolished was because there were no profits. If that were the case no harm would be done by leaving the tax in force. To abolish the tax is simply saying to the business man:	Go
ahead and make all the profits you like, and we will not touch you. That is not sound, in my opinion. I have another quotation to make from the Montreal Star:
"I think the increase in the sales tax will meet with little opposition," states W. M. Birks, 1st vice-president of the Montreal Board of Trade. "It is not so general or uniform a tax as the turnover tax advocated by the Board of Trade, but still It is quite good, as is the abolition of the business war profits tax and the last of the luxury taxes, for which the council of the board has been pressing for some time."
Why are these people so jubilant over this tax? To my mind the reason can be summed up in a word:	They are able
through this new measure of taxation to shift their load on to the other fellow's back.

Mr. Speaker, the Budget debate
has lasted now over a week and has been the means of giving much information to the House and the country at large on the fiscal proposals of the Government. It is certainly with great regret, when I see my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), opposite to me this evening, that I rise in the exercise of what I feel to be my duty to inflict upon him the
burden of my remarks on the Budget. He has delivered his Budget with evident sincerity and honesty, and for that we certainly owe him a debt of gratitude and our congratulations. The fact that he occasionally enunciates good Liberal principles has led me to believe that my hon. friend was a Liberal, but that he has lost his bearings in the befogged economic atmosphere of Toronto. To-day every Canadian is anxious to know what the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) can do to improve our present disquieting financial conditions, and although the Budget which my hon. friend has submitted to Parliament does not contain very much, the facts it discloses are serious enough to set every earnest citizen thinking. It is true that we have passed through very grave and difficult times, but we know, Mr. Speaker, that while our obligations are tremendous, we have resources that are almost inexhaustible; and if the Government would only go about it in the right way, they would find it not an impossible task to put this country once more upon a sound financial basis. I do not minimize the vastness of the task, but I certainly think that the Government is not doing all it can in the present circumstances. For many years to come the people of Canada will have to shoulder a heavy burden in the way of taxation, and it is the duty of whatever Government may be in power to do everything humanly possible, in the way of developing our natural resources, and, above all, of economizing in the management of public affairs, to relieve the people, as far as possible, of that burden. But conditions, I am afraid, seem to be going from bad ' to worse, and this year we have to raise an amount much larger than was called for last year; in addition to which, we must face the increased deficit which is anticipated in connection with the Canadian National Railways. The people to-day are undoubtedly discontented; but, if they had an opportunity of electing a new Parliament, and could feel that that Parliament truly reflected their opinions and their wishes, they would take heart and be fully prepared to co-operate with the Government in the effort to discharge our obligations. Unfortunately, however, as has been remarked on many an occasion, not only the Prime Minister and the Government, but this Parliament as a whole, cannot claim to represent the people. This Parliament was elected under particular circumstances for a specific purpose. Its mandate has expired; the occasion for
| COMMONS

which the Government was returned to office has passed; and the people are anxious to return new representatives who will reflect their views and their wishes, and endeavour to implement their ambitions.
For some considerable time now we have been promised a revision of the tariff, which has been demanded by a section of the press; and if, as some people think, that section is a ininority, still it is a minority that commands the respect of the people. Two years ago we were promised a tariff revision during the recess; and last year the same assurance, in emphatic terms, was given to the House by the Minister of Finance himself. After that assurance I felt convinced that this time there would certainly be a revision of the tariff which we might discuss at this session of Parliament. I am inclined to think that the hon. minister, who travelled from one end of the country to the other, going to the trouble of taking evidence extensively, and of hearing the whole question discussed from every standpoint, must have been personally in favour of undertaking a revision of the tariff. No doubt, however, he has been influenced in his decision by the counsel of his colleagues, and if he finds himself to-day unable to carry out his promise to give us a revision of the tariff, he is not alone responsible. Pressure has been brought to bear upon him, I presume, by the Government and the Prime Minister, and so we hear hon. gentlemen opposite putting forward, as a reason why there is no tariff revision, the importance of our waiting until the United States puts its new tariff law into effect.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Canada would not to-day be faced with any adverse exchange with the United States if we had been wise enough in 911 to adopt the reciprocity agreement proposed by that able leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. That agreement was unquestionably conducive to the greatest prosperity in this country; and, if we had adopted it, it would have made for better conditions financially for Canada, and a very much better mutual understanding between the two countries. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), in 1911, told the people that their only salvation lay in defeating reciprocity; but recently we have seen him pleading with the United States, in that eloquent way we all know, and beseeching them not to use the -weapon in their hands. In 1911, the war cry was "No truck or trade with the Yankees;" to-day it is this:	"Let us be friends; we

are of common origin; there is no reason why we cannot carry on business amicably with each other".
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) the other day, in that virile style of his, criticized the Opposition. I know that he is never at a loss for an argument, but I think he went rather too far when he declared that the tariff we have to-day, under the Conservative party, is identical with the tariff as it was left by my hon. friend, the exMinister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), in 1911. I will admit that the tariff may be the same as was left to hon. gentlemen opposite in 1911-minus the benefits of the reciprocity pact. Those benefits would have been added to the tariff but for the position which my hon. friend and his friends took in regard to reciprocity. Immense benefits would have accrued to Canada under the reciprocity pact to which my hon. friend the ex-Minister o'f Finance had given two years of hard work in order to try and bring the representatives of the American people into harmony with his views and aspirations. Fortunately, there were a couple of provinces in Canada which were not affected by the tornado of prejudice which swept over the country in 1911 and which affected more particularly the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
I refer to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. These two provinces sent a full contingent of representatives to Parliament in support of reciprocity, with the exception perhaps of two gentlemen who have since taken refuge on the bench or elsewhere. Every other representative of the two provinces came to Parliament in the chariot of reciprocity, and not one of them has changed his mind on that important question.
My hon. friends opposite are fond of talking of the value of the home market to the people of Canada. That is the great slogan of the protectionist-the home market. They tell you that you must not consider outside markets or outside conditions; you must confine your activities to the home market. As an illustration of the value of the home market they refer to the article of butter which, during the war, commanded such a high price. Are we not to consider any of the rest of our farm products? What about our wheat and our other grains needed so much by the outside world, and abundant crops of which mean so much to the prosperity of this country? Are we to confine ourselves, in the development of our resources, to a

market of eight or nine millions of people when those resources are such as to enable us to supply the needs of a great part of the world? Where would the wheat grower of the Prairie Provinces be if he were limited to producing only sufficient for the needs of eight or nine millions of people in Canada? Where would be the great benefits to industry, that are now enjoyed, if we had such an extremely restricted market? It is an unrestricted development of production which makes for the prosperity of a nation. We have a country of immense area, and of unlimited resources; and it is in the development of our trade with outside countries that I expect to see Canada grow and expand in the future. Our manufacturers in the big cities should realize this-I think as an actual fact they do realize it-but until they get this broader outlook and act upon it we shall not see Canada expand and prosper in the way she ought to do.
We have seen the luxury taxes as they were called-those taxes which gave so much trouble to the retailers and their customers-discarded and other methods resorted to. But in every case it is the consumer who pays. I have always been in favour of the abolition of taxes that press heavily upon the masses of the people, and replacing them by taxation that would fall upon those best able to meet it. It is not only upon the ordinary commodities that the Minister of Finance is imposing taxes that will bear heavily upon the people-he is now imposing a tax upon lumber. The proposition of the Finance Minister, as outlined in the Budget, reads as follows:
Provided that in respect of lumber an excise tax of three per cent shall be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by the Canadian manufacturers-
This is going to add to the cost of erecting buildings more especially in the cities, and by reason of it tenants will have to pay increased house rents. Only a short time age we heard from the Minister of Railways the statement that owing to the high freight rates we cannot get lumber from British Columbia. Even the people in the prairie district of the West are suffering by reason of that fact. Notwithstanding the prosperity they have been experiencing they will not, owing to the high cost of transportation, be able to obtain lumber from British Columbia to shelter themselves, their families and their stock.
Again, he tells us that that lumber cannot under the present excessive freight rates be transported to Central Canada to meet the needs of the people there. We know also that owing to those same excessive freight rates New Brunswick lumber cannot be sold in Montreal, Toronto or Buffalo as it used to be. Our lumbermen of northern New Brunswick have to pay a freight -rate of $11 per thousand feet to send their lumber to Montreal, and they have to pay another $12 or $13 freight rate to extend their sales to Toronto or Buffalo, which represents the price of the lumber itself. And yet after receiving that statement from the Minister of Railways we find the sales tax on that lumber is increased to three and a half per cent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me? I am sure he would like the facts. Does he know that the two taxes of one per cent each making 2 per cent in all of last year have been consolidated this year in so far as lumber is concerned into a three per cent tax, an increase of one per cent only on the two, and that the rate as consolidated and increased is only 3 and not 31 per cent.

I accept the explanation given by my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton), but still under present conditions if there was one article which should be free of that taxation it is lumber, because in every city there is a dearth of dwelling houses, and the high prices of lumber and other material tend to discourage the erection of new houses.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, the amendment brought in by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) will receive my hearty support, although I think it is well known in this House that I am willing to go much further; but, as I have said on other occasions, we cannot expect free trade to become effective in a moment, especially under present world conditions. It will come gradually as circumstances permit. But certainly the principles underlying that amendment are such as if put into practice will undoubtedly improve' the conditions of our people. The .principle of protection itself is injurious to any country, but especially to such a country as Canada that can only prosper by the development of its natural resources, -that circumstance alone is a sufficient condemnation of protection. The United States is often cited as an example of the benefits accruing from protection, but it must always be remembered that however

high the protective tariff has been in that country, it has never been such a burden upon the people there as is our protective tariff upon our people to-day. But, outside of tariff matters,' permit me to say that the growth and prosperity of the United States cannot be attributed solely, or, indeed, in any degree to their tariff policy, but rather to the expansion of territory which has resulted from successive annexations until the original thirteen New England States have grdwn to over forty, not only increasing the area of the United States but its population also, and those states enjoy a freedom of trade that was unknown to the old colonies. In a word, the industries of the whole country have been developed, and we find that the industrial expansion in California has kept pace with that of New York, while the city of Chicago has become the great centre of commerce of the Middle West, and its unparalleled prosperity has not been at the expense of, but has helped, the prosperity of New York, Boston and Philadelphia.
And my great leader, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, developed this country by revising the tariff to the untold benefit of our people, and by adopting a vigorous immigration policy, he attracted a virile enterprising class of settlers who peopled our western territories, necessitating the creation of new provinces and virtually expanding our territory in a manner somewhat similar to the expansion of the United States. The result has been that the energy of Canadians from the East combined with the energy of our newcomers has developed the West to its present prosperous condition, which has reacted on the East, and this country would not be as well off as it is to-day but for that farsighted policy.
But we are told that we must have protection. I see that the Minister of Labour addressed a meeting a few nights ago at McAdam Junction, and for the time being, apparently, represented himself as the friend of the railway men and of labour generally, and he told them that they must have protection to afford the labouring men plenty of work. In this connection I would remind this House and the country that the working man besides being a seller of labour is also a purchaser of commodities, arid the price of his labour must correspond to the price of the commodities which he has to buy. It is not only a case of for instance a particular manufacturer of boots and shoes, saying to his workmen: "You pay a little more for your boots and shoes
	,
and I will give you higher wages." But after buying their boots and shoes those workmen have also to buy food and clothing for themselves and their families. So we cannot judge of the prosperity of the country merely by a tariff.
This amendment is certainly a move in the right direction-a direction which the late hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier indicated in his manifesto to the people of Canada, in which he said among other things:
If I should he entrusted with th? administration of the country, I would immediately relieve agriculture from all its shackles of the customs duties. Thus I would at once abolish the duties on all farming implements and the other necessities of the farm, and would advocate as an essential object of my administration a general and well constituted reform of the tariff, tending to aid production in Canada and to relieve the Canadian consumer.
This is the programme which would have shaped the destinies of Canada in 1917 had not the people been misled by the flag-waver, and this country would be in a far different position than that in which we find it to-day. Every Canadian, I am sure, will admit that this programme was the best that could be instituted in the interests of Canada, having regard to the conditions. We would have had a degree of free trade which certainly would have satisfied my desire as well as that of every honest free trader in Canada. The same object is embodied in the resolution which has been introduced in amendment by the ex-Minister of Finance, the member for Shelburne and Queen's.
The protectionist spirit, Sir, is not consistent with the principles of democracy. It is the masses of the,people, ninety or ninety-five per cent of the population, who most require assistance. The millionaire can look after himself; it is the man in the factory, the workingman, the man who assists in the development of our natural resources, the man who gets his bread by the sweat of his brow-this is the man whom we should look after. Generally it is he who has the largest family. The object of his affections is at home, and if during the six working days of the week he must worry about how he may provide his family with the necessities of life, he cannot enjoy his home on Sunday. To improve the condition of these people should be the aspiration of every man who has to do with the administration of the country's affairs, and this applies not only to Canada but to every other nation. Henry George once said that the spirit of love, not hate, will produce happiness; that it knows no difference of race or creed; it knows no animosities. That,

Mr. Speaker, is the spirit of free trade, and whether or not we can put it into practice in toto, it is the spirit which should animate the people of Canada to-day.
I listened with great attention this afternoon to the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) with regard to the condition of the workingman. He said he would have the workingman prosper; he even said they should enjoy a portion of the benefits accruing to the businesses for which they were working. I consider myself a greater free trader than the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville. I do not go so far as he does, but I do say that we should do all we can to bring happiness and contentment to the workingman, and only by enabling him to obtain under fair conditions the commodities which he must purchase for the sustenance of his family can we hope to make him happy and contented. If we make the workingman happy and contended he will rise in the esteem of the whole people; his work will contribute to the prosperity of the nation and he will be glad to do an honest day's work for whatever wage he gets.
With regard to the question of revenue, I submit that the raising of what I might call indirect revenue means the placing of the burden upon the masses of the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite express their approval of the income tax. It is true that we have had income tax for the last three years, but I may point out that the provision for income tax, while put into effect by hon. gentlemen opposite, is the work of the Liberal party. We had almost exhausted our patience in asking for it, and the Government had exercised all its powers of resistance against it. I and other gentlemen on this side from the very beginning of the war urged that we should have income tax and thus avoid borrowing in order to meet the expenses of the war. But during three years of the war, when the greatest prosperity prevailed in Canada, when immense profits were made and such a source of revenue would have yielded two or three times what it brings to-day, the Government took no action. Of course, the present Finance Minister is not responsible, for he was not here at the time. I am sure that if he had been here, he would, in his generosity of heart, have inspired his colleagues to better sentiments in this direction. However, I repeat that the Liberal party through its constant efforts in that regard is responsible for the introduction of this tax.	-
We are told that we must have a tariff; that a tariff alone can save the country. But look at the case of Great Britain. During the last sixty or seventy-five years she has had free trade and she has expanded her commerce so greatly that the English language is recognize^ to-day as the language of trade and commerce. Her trade has reached every shore and every ocean, and the principle of free trade, recognized by Great Britain, has been the means of engendering a spirit of fraternity and encouraging true Christian sentiments. It is the policy which has created Britain's great merchant navy-and it is to be remembered that it was Britain's navy which won the war and without which the victory could not have been ours. Surely that is a circumstance which should impress every nation.
On different occasions in this House the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) has referred to hon. gentlemen on this side as Bolshevists and wreckers. As I and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) have on many occasions in this House set forth the principles of free trade, I must be included in the reference which my right hon. friend made, in which hon. gentlemen advocating the policy of free trade were called Bolshevists and wreckers.

speechtext: Get somebody to quote what I said.

I am not so far away from the truth after all. I am not converted for all that to the principle of protection, and I sincerely believe in this great policy which is bound to be adopted in Canada, because, if there is in the world a country which has been made, by Providence, a country which should have free trade, it is certainly Canada with her mag-

nificent natural resources and her markets on every ocean and on every side. We can reach the countries on the Pacific ocean as well as those on the Atlantic. When I speak in favour of a diminution of the tariff as rapidly as possible, I do not think the result will be to injure the manufacturer. I have no objection to the prosperity of the manufacturer; I desire that he should prosper; and when I advocate an expansion of trade into the great markets of the world, my desire is to ensure his prosperity, for I say that the Canadian manufacturer will never prosper as he should, with the resources that he has at his command, until he has developed his trade with other nations, whether on the European continent or in the Orient. When I say that we can do with a lower tariff, I do not mean that I want to harm either the manufacturer, the employer or the employee. A protective tariff is bad, as everyone who will study the matter will admit; a tariff for revenue is better, but no tariff at all is better still. Let me prove my contention by this argument. We say that we must have revenue, and to get revenue we must have importation. You cannot have revenue unless you import. The more revenue you wish to collect by a tariff, the more you must encourage importation, and the more you deprive the labourer of his work and the manufacturer of his products. Supposing we collect $200,000,000 by a tariff. That represents a total importation of, say, $800,000,000. Therefore, it means $800,000,000 worth of commodities that the labourer has not been able to work upon and that the manufacturer has not been able to produce in this country. Therefore, the more you encourage revenue by importation, the more you deprive the workmen and the manufacturer of their prosperity.
This is a time when the people of Canada should encourage freer trade between the nations in order to restore harmony, more particularly between nations on the European continent and some other continents where agitation still exists in the minds of the people. This can be done by opening the doors to their commerce and asking those countries to join with us in trade as well as in other matters. Trade creates friendship, and with friendship we shall have peace. With animosity, we shall have war.
The Brussels Conference was referred to by the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in a speech which he delivered in presenting his amendment. I should, how-

ever, like to read over again the two resolutions which he quoted from that conference, in order to impress more deeply upon the House the consequences which I draw for Canada from them. This is what the first one says:
The Conference recommends that within such limits and at such time as may appear possible each country should aim at the progressive restoration of that freedom of commerce which prevailed before the war, including the withdrawal of artificial restrictions on, and discriminations of price against, external trade.
Another resolution is this:
The International Financial Conference affirms that the improvement of the financial position largely depends on the general restoration as soon as possible of good-will-between the various nations; and in particular it endorses the declaration of the Supreme Council of the 8th March last "that the States which have been created or enlarged as a result of the war should at once re-established full and friendly co-operation and arrange for the unrestricted interchange of commodities in order that the essential unity of European economic life may not be impaired by the erection of artificial economic barriers."
Such is the proposition laid down by those resolutions of the Brussels Conference at which the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) represented Canada, and I am proud that a representative of Canada gave his adherence to such resolutions, the putting into effect of which would fill my heart with joy
9 p.m. and happiness, because I would see, in the near future, happiness and contentment in the various nations of the world. It is an invitation which, certainly, the people of Canada should not only accept with great pleasure, but endeavour to enforce upon other nations. Let Canada do her duty to-day "as she did it at the beginning of and during the war. As in those days, love of the Mother Country, Great Britain, was able to bring from every ocean her millions of subjects and to unite them into one common bond under the beneficent smile of Providence, let again the same spirit animate us all in every clime, and in every country; let us here to-day, unite in the endeavour to promote peace, harmony, and good-will amongst the nations of the earth. We have been told that Canada is a great nation; that she enjoys a reputation beyond that of any of the greater nations owing to the sacrifices which she made in the war and the intelligent service rendered by our Canadian soldiers. If Canada is a nation big enough to be a member of the league, let her be a member big enough to be a leader in that league.

Let us to-day put aside our prejudices and start in the direction of freer trade with other countries, so that we may be sure we shall not be confronted with another war in the future. We are asked, what else are you going to do? I say: Reduce the tariff so that our people may be able to buy the necessaries of life and educate their children, who certainly in the course of time will be the rulers of the country. We all know that very often from the families of the working men come those who are destined for the highest places in the world.
I have already on more than one occasion given my ideas on a system of taxation which is not new to this Parliament. I have dilated on that scheme very often and perhaps I should not touch upon it to-night, but I read a reference to it, not being present in the House, in the speeches of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and my hon. friend from Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Thomson). I refer to a land values tax. I again advocate that system of taxation. I want it to be well understood that I am not advocating a tax on improvements to property, but merely on the unearned increment. The local Government are to-day raising revenue by the taxation of property, but they are taxing the improvements. I do not advocate that. I want only that land to be taxed that is unemployed, and that is being held mainly for the purpose of exacting a higher price. It is the mere value of the land itself that we should tax, and not the improvements, for that would be an injustice to the people of Canada. In any country the value of the land rises with the improvements and the general prosperity of the country. The construction of a railway or of public works in any portion of Canada causes the land in the neighbourhood to rise in value, and this added value that is given to the land should be for the benefit and prosperity of the whole country. To-day the farmer who has 100 acres of land upon which he works hard finds that the more buildings he erects and the more improvements he makes to his property the more he is taxed, while (he farmer alongside of him who allows his land to lie uncultivated pays no tax at all. It is the land of this farmer, who is leaving his farm unused, without any benefit to the people of the community, that we wish to tax. And similarly with regard to the land in the cities. We do not wish to tax the improvements, but the vacant land that is
being held for a higher price. If you tax that land, the owner seeks either to use it or to sell it. As I said, land values rise with the improvements in the neighbourhood and the general prosperity of the country, and it is certainly astonishing sometimes to see how greatly values rise. Every time I walk along Sparks street I am struck by the immense value of its property-a value which has been given to it by the Federal Government of Canada. What was the value of a foot of land on Sparks street or Bank street about fifty years ago before the creation of a Capital in Ottawa? Not very much. Since the session opened I saw in the newspapers that a piece of property with a thirty-three foot frontage on Sparks street, without a building on it, had been purchased by the Home Bank for $195,000. How much would that land have been worth if the seat of Parliament was not in Ottawa? Only about $400 or $500. The increased value has been given it by the Federal Government being in Ottawa and having erected buildings here, with all the necessary improvements in the neighbourhood. These improvements have meant that a piece of land that otherwise would have been worth only a few hundred dollars is now worth $195,000. If we have to raise $200,000,000 of revenue, we would have to raise from the city of Ottawa, I suppose, about $2,000,000 or $3,000,000, according to population. How much better it would be if we could help to raise that amount by taxing the land values in the way I have suggested, instead of raising the money by going into the home of the working man, the clerk, the school teacher, and the returned soldier, and extorting the tax from their tables and upon the things they wear. That is the difference between the two methods of taxation. A land values tax such as I have advocated will not interfere with exchange or transportation or with any other business. After all, this land value taxation is an old British Liberal principle. You can find that principle as far back as William the Conqueror, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance knows I am right. William the Conqueror took possession of all the land and parcelled it out amongst his generals and officers and soldiers on the condition that they would always be prepared for military service. During this great man's reign the common people had no regular taxes to pay in connection with wars; the nobility were always in a state of preparedness. It was

only afterwards, when they refused to discharge their obligations, that the common people suffered and pauperism got a footing in Britain. The principle which I have stated is one that Campbell-Bannerman, Asquith, and Lloyd George advocated before the war, although Lloyd George of late has betrayed it. Even at the rate of one per cent we could raise a very large revenue by taxing unused lands, and by that means we could raise revenue instead of taking it out of the working classes, who find it difficult enough to provide themselves and their families with food and clothing. The sooner we have a Government that will introduce a system of this sort, the better it will be for the whole country. If this were done, the working classes would be grateful to the party that brought it about. Extravagance at any time is wrong, but to-day particularly it is criminal, and I think we can safely claim that the Conservative Government and its successors, since 1911, have been wasting the people's money. Now, I think that one way of putting an end to extravagance would be to tax land values. If this were done, the land-owners would themselves see to it that there was no extravagance on the part of the Government, entailing an increase in taxes in which they'would participate; and I suggest this as one of the best policies that could be adopted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have perhaps kept the House too long. I regret my inability to place before you and before the country, the views which I hold on many subjects. Were I gifted with the eloquence, the impressiveness, and the clear expression of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), or of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), I would use that gift in submitting, not only to the members of this House, but to the people of the country at large, the views which I have for the betterment of conditions in this country, and the opinions which, I think, if put into practice, would at least help towards the general prosperity. My opinions may not be acceptable to many hon. members, but I state them, nevertheless; and, as I say, my only regret is that I cannot express myself with the clearness which I should desire. I believe that there are many things which the Government could do to help the country out of its present difficulty, and I only wish they would do these things. In conclusion, Sir, I trust that the House will pardon me for having taken so much time in giving expression

to the principles of British Liberalism which I have stated to-night, and which I think are the only right principles in the present conditions, not only in Canada, but throughout the world.
