Hon. gentlemen must remember that it is the American people who tell us what we can sell in their country, and it is the Canadian people who tell them what they can sell in our country. It has been said by economists that one of the most useful purposes to which a tariff can be put is that of a weapon for bargaining. It enables you to say: We will trade you this for that so long as it does not injure any interest that is neces-say to our country or injure any of our institutions. A country like Canada, with eight millions of people, that would adopt free trade with the highest protected country in the world at her doors, with a population of one hundred and ten millions, would be committing national hari-kari, or a crime, call it by any other name you will, that would put her out of existence in the twinkling of an eye.
Having said that much, may I suggest to the Government-I know the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) will not agree with this, for this matter has been mentioned in the House before- that at the present time they should look a little forward in regard to our own trade problems. Internally, I think, Canada has weathered the storm pretty well. I think she is entitled to be proud of the sanity and level-headedness of her people, but at certain times in our history I believe there is a duty upon Government to do a little more than probably they would do in ordinary times. In that connection I want to point out that last year the United States sold to Canada over $1,000,000,000 of their products, while we sold to the United States about $552,000,000; that is, the United States, with 110,000,000 people, sold $2 worth of goods to us, while Canada, with a population of 8,000,000, sold $1 worth to them. Our trade stands out very prominently there, because one might have expected that a country like the United States with their gigantic industrial system, their large organizations and their much greater population, would have sold their goods to us in a greater proportion than two to one, hut thanks to our tariff we have held them to a reasonable basis. If we had free trade, they would sell to. us every dollar's worth of goods that we wanted, and this country would go out of business industrially. The United States has adopted a different position from ours. They went after Canadian trade, but Canadians did not go after American trade. This $552,000,000 of Canadian goods was 
sold to the United States without Canada trying to sell them. What I means is this:	the United States has
in this country ninety-two consuls-general, consular agents and trade agents. For the benefit of the House I would refer to the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs of this Government, for the year ending March 31, 1920. At page 9, appendix A, of that report you will find the names of all the American consuls in this country. They have two or three in Montreal and Toronto, several in Vancouver, and in all our cities from Halifax to Vancouver there is either an American consul-general, an American vice-consul, or an American trade agent. We have not a blessed one in the' United States 'with its market of 110,000,000 people, while they have 92 in this country. What for? Why, to look after the interests oi the United States in Canada. I repeat, we have not one to look after our trade interests in the United; States. These- consular agencies of the United States in' this country have put themselves on a selfsustaining basis. Under their regulations every shipment of goods from this country to the United States must be accompanied by a fee for viseing the invoice. In the eight years from 1913 to 1920 there have been collected from the Canadian people in these fees on Canadian shipments to the United States the sum of $2,595,326.92. The total expenditure for Canada was $1,630,823.80. Thus, the consular agents of the United States, out of these fees from Canadian pockets in these eight years, have made a profit over all overhead charges for the maintenance and upkeep of their oflices in Canada of $964,503.12.

But the question which I should like to have , answered is, why Canada has no trade agents there while Britain has 115. I do not suggest that the commercial activities of Great Britain would be pursued and developed at the expense of Canada. I have never heard it suggested that this should be done, and I cannot conceive it to be so; but I will venture, without fear of successful contradiction, the statement that the British trade
agent is looking especially after British trade and not Canadian; and our trade would be greatly increased if we had in the United States, commensurate with their population, a staff of trade agents from Seattle or San Francisco to New York, and down to the Gulf of Mexico, and throughout the Eastern States. If we had, in every important city of the American union, a corps of properly trained agents skilled in business methods, we should be able to extend our trade with the United States, to an extent hardly conceivable, and where we sell $552,000,000 worth of goods in a year, without special effort, the amount we could sell, if we did try through the work of trained agents, would he so great, in spite of a tariff which might be prohibitive in some respects, that it would redound to the everlasting welfare of this great Dominion. We have trade agents in Asia and Europe, so that the principle is not new. Now, what other benefit would there be from having trade agents in the United States to look after Canadian interests? In the first place, if the United States in Canada, with a consulate service numbering 92, can make nearly $1,000,000 a year more than it costs to maintain the service, surely it is not too much to say that Canada, with a service of equal strength, could make a million and a half dollars more than would pay the way of these trade agents, in view of the fact that their trade shipments are greater to Canada than ours to the United States. The trade agents would be live wires, because, of course, you would have to send none but live wires. There are hundreds of young men, commercial travellers and business men, in this country who I believe could do wonderful work if this policy were adopted. Indeed, there are thousands of them and they are of the brightest minds we have in business and trade. Let them go over. If we have an ambassador there, all well and good; but if I had my choice between an ambassador on the one hand, and a number of trade agents on the other, I would elect for the trade agents every time, and leave the ambassadorial work to the British Embassy. Let us get into the British ways of trade expansion and "go to it" as a young man would say. These trade agents located there would be active and energetic and would prevent smuggling into this country, because every invoice would have to be vised and would pass through their hands. I deem it my duty on rising to congratulate the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Morphy) on the thoroughly efficient manner in which he extolled the Government's action and policy. I am not at all surprised at the hon. gentlemen's eulogy; I think he still hopes to enter the Cabinet in which there are yet " rooms to let." I imagine his object in making so lengthly a speech must have been to qualify himself for a portfolio.
The hon. member for North Perth dwelt on the importance of having Canada represented by trade agents in the United States. This policy was first advocated by a former member for St. James, Montreal, the late Honore Gervais, who for many years favoured such a course in this House. What Canada needs at the present time is not an ambassador at Washington for ceremonial purposes but a real business man to develop trade with our great neighbour' to the south.
I am certain that nobody in this chamber will refuse the Minister of Finance the admiration which he deserves for his courage in the presentation of such a poor Budget. For my part, I do not deny him my warmest sympathy in the thankless task which he had in explaining to the country the lamentable state of affairs for which the present Government is responsible.
Lamentable, it is in reality, Mr. Speaker, for to the enormous debt under which the tax-payer is already overburdened, one must add the trifle of over one hundred million dollars for this year, despite the promises made last year by the Minister of Finance that the national debt would be reduced.
I doubt very much if, when he made this consoling promise, the Minister of Finance had taken the time to measure the incompetance of the Government into which he was invited to enter. Had he done so he would have maintained a prudent silence, instead of blaming inwardly those who drew him into this chaos where now hs finds himself with his unfortunate though honourable colleagues.
How far are we, Mr. Speaker, from those blessed times when, after twelve months of fruitful administration, the honourable member for Shelburne' and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), then Minister of Finance of the Liberal Government, unrolled before the amazed eyes of the country the spectacle of the prosperity existing from one end of the country to the other, the spectacle of peace and concord reigning among employers and employees. How far we are, Mr. Speaker, from that happy time when we saw every factory in the country smoking night and day and where we saw our dear Canada advancing by giant strides towards her destiny, under the vigorous impulsion of our ever to be regretted chief, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
To destroy this magnificent work ten years have sufficed, Mr. Speaker, of a government born in 1911 of the alliance, justly called immoral, of the Tories with a handful of political adventurers disguised as Nationalists, wrecks of the two parties who were thrown on the reefs of the indignation of their compatriots.
I can quite understand, Mr. Speaker, that the right honourable predecessor of the present Prime Minister, oppressed with a sense of discouragement and fright at the sight of the ruins of his party, might have wished to throw on the shoulders of the right honourable member for Portage-la-Prairie the weight of the universal repror

bation under which the Canadian electorate proposes to smother the present Government at the next general elections; for, it would be just that -the right hon. Prime Minister, principal author of these fatal politics, should- behold their disastrous consequences.
If now, Mr. Speaker, we cast a glance at the state of our finances, we are amazed to find that not only has our debt not diminished, but it has increased, as I indicated a moment ago, to the truly colossal sum of two billion three hundred and fifty millions; and if we seek the cause of this increase, we find it in the foolish policies of the Government, which, since 1911, has clung to power iby means of all possible concessions;-policies, foolish and disastrous, I repeat, chiefly in three cases: An imprudently immoderate participation in the European war, costing us the loss of millions and millions of dollars, which otherwise would be available now; absurd railway policies which have this year absorbed one hundred and thirteen millions of dollars; and, finally, unlimited waste, added to the improvidence of a Government which has done nothing to guard us against the labour crisis at present raging throughout the country, the reverberations of which are shaking the economical structure of the nation.
J was in favour, Mr. Speaker, of reason-ab.e and limited participation in the European war, but I absolutely disapprove of the manner in which the Government conducted it. Instead of enriching certain of their favourites with millions through large war contracts, why did they not take over, for instance, the control of the manufacture of munitions, even if it were necessary, as in the case of the erection of this Parliament building, for example, to allow a percentage of reasonable profit to the different firms having charge of the manufacture of munitions for the account of the Canadian Government, thus saving to the state 'millions which were scandalously wasted to gorge the pockets of a few personages in the good graces of the Government.
The right hon. the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, has a right to be pleased with his work-he, who, in 1915, swore to spend up to the last cent of the treasury, even if it was necessary to bring the country into bankruptcy. I spoke a little while ago of the railway policy of the Government.
It is not surprising to us on this side of the House that the country is facing disaster; from the moment, when, by a turn [Mr. L,educ.J
of the hand, the right hon. chief of the Government, instead of asking the administrators of the private railways the secret of good direction, bought the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk, it was to be foreseen that the same disorder, the same contempt for the safeguard of the money of the Canadian people, the same wild dance of dollars would bring us rapidly to the regrettable'situation in ,which we find ourselves to-day, by the accumulation of annual deficits. But, how to get out of this mix-up, Mr. Speaker? I would suggest to the right hon. the Prime Minister that this should be put before the committee appointed to consider these questions, and the suggestions made by that capable business man, Lord Sh-aughnessy, should be taken into serious consideration.
I may quote, Mr. Speaker, an article from the Financial Times of January 29 last on a speech delivered by Sir Herbert Holt at the annual meeting of the Royal Bank of Canada, which reads as follows:
"Government control has practically disappeared during the year just past-wheat, papei and sugar being the commodities to be freed from regulation. Government ownership of transportation systems has developed. Without any advantage to the public in efficiency or rates, the operation of our national railways during the past twelve months has resulted in a loss which will probably more than absorb the amounts collected on excess profits and income taxes for the year 1919. Unless Government methods of operation are more efficient in this country than they have been in others, tax payers in Canada may find the maintenance of their railroads and fleet more expensive than pension charges and other legacies of the war combined."
These few sentences constitute one of the most graphic denunciations of the evils of government ownership it has been our privilege to read in a long time. Time was when the mention of millions almost took our breath away. A millionaire was as well worth seeing as a crowned head. It was not necessary to gfl beyond millions to express the superlative of all things. The war ruined our perspective. We began to talk of millions as though they were merely thousands. It is no longer -possible to waken the Canadian public to a realization of what government operation of railways may cost by expressing it in figures. What if it does cost $50,000,000 or $75,000,000 per annum? The Finance Minister will borrow it or dig it up in some manner. The cost does not seem to come home to us. We will pay it along with other costs and grouch about our heavy taxation and let the government continue to extend it field of operations. We will ask it to loan us more money to bulid houses witih and to finance other operations or interfere in other matters of business which we should be attending to ourselves and which will only result in further deficits and increased taxation.
President Holt of the Royal Bank, however, avoids much reference to figures. Instead, he tells us that government operation of our railways will probably result in a loss which will

exceed the governmental revenue from excess profits and income taxes. Could anything bring this matter home to us in more vivid manner? The whole business world denounces the excess profits tax and practically everyone who pays an Income tax does so with rage in his heart against the German junker who is supposed to have laid him under the levy.
But, here, in Canada, and altogether independent of the war, is a levy which we, as good democrats and as electors with the freedom of the ballot, have placed upon ourselves. The excess profits tax and the income tax go to wipe out the annual defiicit of our governmental system of railways. Nay, the situation is yet worse. This whole burden of increased tatxation which we laJbor under promises to go finally but to wipe out the annual loss incurred in the operation of our railways We are not paying the interest on our war bill with it at all, we are not even paying pensions

we are just breaking even-on governmental operation of our railways. Presumably this means we will have to tax ourselves all over againt to pay for the war. Truly it is a condition of affairs of which we have little reason to feel proud.
As long as the Government persists in its nefarious policy of helping certain gangs of financiers-if I may use the expression, Mr.	Speaker-interested	in the maladministration of the railways, by administering them in the worst possible manner, the Canadian people must hold themselves ready to meet the growing deficits from year to year. I have been asking myself, Mr. Speaker, how the Minister of Finance could make up his Budget this year without borrowing. There remains to him, it is true, the imposition of new taxes. As to that, the Canadian people would have little to say if the Government would divide the burden equitably and proportionately to the re sources of each class and of each individual. I understand that again this year the Government is following the detestable custom it followed during the war, wheu it placed its rapacious hand on the shoulder of the small contributor, the man who had brought up a large family only to make food for cannon, while it exempted those who rested comfortably at the fireside and amassed exorbitant profits. Following this policy, the Government has lifted the tax on luxuries, which, to my mind, was a just tax. It has also abolished the tax on profits, thus lightening the burden of the rich, very often with few if any children, and shifting it to the poor, frequently the supporters of large families. Further, the only capital which should have been spared -the human capital furnished by these numerous families and which in the end, constitutes the wealth of the nation-was again this year particularly hit for the benefit of capial held in the hands of a minority which compromises by its monopoly the equilibrium of the country.
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, let this occasion pass without saying a few words about the high cost of living, which has regularly increased every year under the placid eyes of the Government-a Government more occupied in conducting throughout the country a campaign of racial hate to ensure its return to power than in giving attention to matters of this kind. While the humble labourer was asking himself how he was going to meet the needs of his family, the profiteers and monopolists of all kinds were occupying themselves in artificially raising the cost of living and hastening to protect their fortunes by buying up nearly a billion and a half of Victory bonds-free from taxes through the imprudence of the Government-and openly defying the Board of Commerce, the institution supposed to be designed to regulate their profits. Mr. Speaker, if I were to enumerate all the errors accumulated by the incompetence of the Government during the time it has had charge of the country's affairs it would be necessary for me to retain the attention of this chamber for a much longer time than I intend to occupy.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to protest in advance in the most vehement manner possible against any attempt to change anything which touches the actual state of our foreign relations or to involve us in new military or naval expenses outside of our country without the unanimous consent of this House? I allude to the next Imperial Conference, in which the Government has given itself carte blanche to take part. Too often our autonomy has been sacrificed at these Imperial conferences and heavy burdens imposed upon us under the pretext of our being admitted to the rank of sister nation. Too long the Imperial statesmen have tired our ears and fascinated our eyes with the words "equality" and "sister nation", while they sacrificed our children, exploited our finances and endangered our liberty. Before we become embroiled to our great detriment in Imperial affairs, let us remember that our country is Canada and that no others than Canadians can ensure her prosperity and future.

The hon. Minister of Finance told us recently that he had abolished the war profits tax, because, said he, large companies shall not have any more immense profits and shall not pay another cent. But you are quite aware that these large companies have divided up their capital in three or four parts and that instead of paying any dividends on a share which was originally worth $100 or $200, the apparent value of these shares has been raised to four or five hundred dollars. Are you not witnesses that these large companies-they are friends of the Government, you may say- have changed their capital stock, that they have quadrupled, quintupled this capital, this being done, the dividend must also be quintupled. It is not surprising therefore that it is as much as large companies can do to pay their dividends or even to pay a part of their profits to the public treasury. The hon. minister had it in his power to prevent these large companies from subdividing their stock. Why has he not done so? If he had acted thus he might have obliged these gentlemen, his friends, to pay into the public treasury a part of the wealth they have extorted from the public during the war; but he could not do so, because they were his friends and he had to protect them. Therefore the Minister of Finance is to blame if the Government's friends are not paying the taxes as they should.
The hon. member from Neepawa (Mr. Davis) remarked the other day that while taxes had been abolished for large companies, nothing had been done to amend the income tax so far as smaller companies were concerned. It is these small companies in the province of Quebec and the western provinces which usually manufacture the agricultural implements which our farmers need, and these small companies which did not come under the war profits tax, had to pay the income tax. By leaving the income tax such as it is, these small companies which are capitalized at less than $25,000, are still subject to a tax. An exemption of $2,000 is allowed on their capital, and any amount in excess of this shall be taxed 10 per cent; as in the past. Yet, they are forced to sell their products at 3 per cent like the others. This makes it impossible for the smaller companies to continue their business and it places them almost on the
verge of bankruptcy. It is an indirect way of doing away with the small competitor, he who very often succeeds in making the large companies, who are friends of the Government, reduce their prices. The hon. Minister of Finance has veiled these details in the Budget. It is the consumer who, in the end will have to pay; it is he who shall have to meet the large deficits of this Government which the people did not want, this Government which has proclaimed itsel! "the country's Government" and which, however hard the Opposition has tried, it has not been able to bring them to their senses and have them bring on the elections.
I had the pleasure the other day to hear the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballan-tyne) claim the candidate from Yamaska as his worthy adopted son, also as that of his leader, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen). Now that the child has been recognized, that he is to be christened -for he is in the county of Yamaska to be christened-I shall take the liberty of asking a question:	Who are the ministers
who are entitled to vote in the county of Yamaska? Could the hon. Minister of Justice tell me if there are any? Could the hon. Minister of Marine tell me if there are any ministers who are entitled to vote in Yamaska? The hon. Minister of Marine does not wish to answer. It might be interesting to know. We might then know, now that the hon. minister has accepted the son, who is to show him the way in the county of Yamaska? According to the law, all ministers must reside in Ottawa; yet there is a minister who has found means of registering in Yamaska so that he as well as his own family, may cast a vote in that county. Could the Government allow a minister, according to the law, to vote in Yamaska, when he has lived in the city of Ottawa since 1911? The Postmaster General (Mr. Blondin) has found out that he could vote in that county, as well as could all his family.
I have in my possesion for the personal edification of my hon. friend and to replace the answer which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries refused to give me, the proof that the Postmaster General intends to vote in the constituency of Yamaska. One father has owned up to the child, but the other supposed father-when one is a putative father, there may be several-will try to mark out the way for him. In the parish of St. Francois-du-Lac, there appears on the electoral list the name of the Hon. P. E. Blondin, senator,

Postmaster General, and it has been put there on the special request of the minister himself. Although he is a resident of the city of Ottawa, this gentleman's name has been inscribed on the electoral list of the parish of St. Franeois-du-Lac. Not satisfied with his name being placed on the list he has seen that the name of Madam P. E. Blondin be added to the electoral list. Then, the hon. minister said to himself: Why should not the name of my sister-inlaw be added also? And the name of Miss E. Brisson, sister-in-law of the hon. Postmaster General has been added on the electoral list of the parish of St. Francois-du-Lac, notwithstanding -the fact that she lives in the city of Ottawa. Miss Marie Brisson too, another sister-in-law of the hon. minister has found a way, thanks probably to her charming brother-in-law, to obtain for herself the right to vote in the constituency of Yamaska, although she resides in Ottawa. Arthur Brisson, civil engineer-a rather interesting thing for his friends in the Mines Branch-also an official of the State residing in Ottawa, found it possible to have a right to vote in the same county. Moreover, the name of Miss Josephine Blondin, a cousin of the hon. Postmaster General, now employed as a stenographer for the Federal Government in Ottawa, figures also on the electoral list of St. Francois-du-Lae, making in all six members of the Blondin family, all residents of Ottawa, who have a right to vote in the constituency of Yamaska. Therefore, this is why I have asked the hon. Minister of Justice as well as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who fortunately understand very well the French language, if to their knowledge some of their colleagues had the right of vote in the county of Yamaska. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries discovered the candidate and has claimed him. Well, the Postmaster General for his own part will despatch him by mail on May the 28th, but, Sir, to the dead-letter branch. When one realizes the ways and means taken by the members of this Government in order to assure the election of their candidates and how they can twist the law in view of securing a right to vote in a constituency where they do not reside and where they simply go for an automobile tour during the summer, have we not the right to ask you to what excess you, as well as your colleagues are ready to descend in view of securing votes?

Now, I desire to make a few remarks concerning the way the hon. Minister of Finance deals with the railways' deficits. I believe that the best way for my hon. friend to cover these deficits of our Canadian National railways is to remain silent cm that score. In the long run it is "Baptiste" that pays. Do you want an illustration, gentlemen, about the bad administration of the national railways?

speechtext: I will remind the hon. member once again that he is speaking in the House of Commons and that he must address the Chair.

The Department of Railways is administered in such a way that the present state of things is of evil omen for the country. The Government, not satisfied with having dragged the Canadian Northern Railway System to bankruptcy, has taken into its service the leading officials of that railway. How could we expect, Mr. Speaker, that the administration of this road would sustain many changes at the hands of these people?
I claim that it is not so, and we become absolutely sure of it when we see what is going on around us. Let me specially draw your attention, for instance, to the manner in which the express companies are being dealt with. There are two great ex-

press companies in this country: the Dominion Express, which is the sole property of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canadian Express, which belongs to the Government. As you follow the Intercolonial frormMontreal along to St. Rosalie, Drummondville, Levis, Montmagny, Riviere du Loup up to Rimouski, you will notice a most extraordinary state of things. We have here a Government who accepted to take over a company with a capital of $1,000,000 and which has $4,000,000 of debentures on the market. That makes a capital of $5,000,000. In every station of the Intercolonial the agent of the Dominion Express is the station master who is in the employ of the Government, while our own company, the Canadian Express, must seek refuge outside of the station. Who has to suffer for this? Who has to pay for the transfer of the goods from the station to the offices? It is the people, it is the company itself. Here is a striking example:	In
the town of Montmagny, which has a population of 5,000, both companies are represented. The station agent of the Canadian National railways is the representative of the Dominion Express, and the latter's packages are received in the offices of the station agent. Now, what is being done with regard to the Canadian Express? The goods are left on the platform of the station and the company has to pay somebody to bring them over to the offices which it had to rent in the town, and also to deliver them to the people at the same rate as the Dominion Express. It means that in the town of Montmagny alone, the Canadian Express is losing every year $500 or $600, which it could save, if conditions were reversed. Why should not the Canadian Express, which is our oVvn company, be represented at the station? Why do they not compel the Dominion Express to transfer its offices elsewhere and to pay for the carriage of its goods? In that way we could get our full revenue and we would be able to save millions on the whole system if the Government would only manage the roads in the proper way. But they don't want to do it; they gave the Canadian Pacific privileges which they do not care to take away from that company.
One of the hon. members opposite, speaking on behalf of the manufacturers, said that if we wanted to reduce our deficits and be able to pay off our debts, we should encourage our industries and buy "made in Canada" goods. Do you know, Sir, who originated this war-cry and who first urged upon the people of Canada to buy Canadianmade goods in preference to, the imported ones? It is the manufacturer himself. If we, the consumers, must buy Canadian goods, we have a right to know whether the manufacturers are themselves setting the example in patronizing Canadian industries and Canadian financial undertakings and also in buying as much as possible of their materials in Canada. To illustrate my thought and to show that these people are not quite the patriots they would like us to believe they are, I made inquiries as to how much insurance, either against fire, or employer's liabilities, or as security bonds, they were taking in the various Canadian companies, and also how much they were taking in British and foreign firms. In 1919, fire insurance policies in Canada amounted to $40,031,474. Out of that sum, the Canadian companies only held $6,415,838; the British companies, $20,377,871, and foreign firms, $13,237,765. Therefore, out of $40,000,000 worth of insurance carried in this country, only six millions were placed with Canadian companies, and thirty-three millions were held by companies having their head office and shareholders outside of Canada. If you consider the difference between the amount collected every year as premiums and that paid out by the companies, you will realize that we are paying a tribute of some fifteen or eighteen millions to strangers every year. Now, who are the people holding the largest fire insurance policies in Canada? It is surely not the farmer nor the poor consumer who very often is not insured, it is the financial corporations. Why do they not apply to the Canadian companies to get insured? Why do they not set the example of encouraging the Canadian companies? Their support would make those companies more powerful, that money would remain in the country and the whole community would profit by it. In 1919, the respective amounts of insurance taken in the Canadian, British and foreign companies against accidents were according to order as follows: $953,103, $1,199,036 and $388,009. Why should those people not get their workingmen insured in Canadian companies, when they are so loud in their utterances to the effect that goods made in Canada, should be given preference?
If you wish to see another aspect of this question, I shall give you the figures on cattle which are specially for the farmer's use. In 1919, $65,657 worth of insurance [DOT]on Canadian herds was taken in Canadian companies and $32,942 in the British companies, foreign companies having done no



business because they were not represented with fespect to that kind of insurance, and this is to our farmer's credit. Though the figures just quoted be not very high, we see, however, that our good country people go so far, at least, as to apply those principles by favouring their fellow-citizens rather than foreigners. Mr. Chairman, if the manufacturers, who are always complaining that they are not protected as much as they should be, were willing to apply the principles which they preach, our financial situation would not be what it is to-day, the one-half of our people would not be taxed for the benefit of the other half.
The ministry in power has not the support of the people, all the by-elections went against them. They are afraid to face the storm and they put off, as much as possible, holding elections in the constituencies which are not represented in the House of Commons, and I can safely assure you that if the Government decided to do what the Prime Minister gave us to understand, the other day, that we might anticipate, the event alluded to by the Ottawa Journal this morning, the Prime Minister would take the place of the leader of the Opposition, which is rightfully his, because he should lead the opposition for a long time before he is Prime Minister.

When he went out of power the tariff averaged 26.7 per cent.
Evidently the right hon. gentleman has revised some of his figures of last year.

Mr. STEVENS': What the Prime Minister stated was that 28.65 was the average duty in the 15 years of the Liberal regime, and 26.7 per cent the lowest rate of duty or the duty at the time the Liberal Government went out of office.

The hon. gentleman has just told us that 28.65 per cent was the average duty in the 15 years of the Liberal regime. The words that were used by the Prime Minister are these, as will be seen by Hansard of last year:
The next year the percentage was 28.65.

There is no average for fifteen years about that. It is the percentage for the year. Therefore, I cannot accept the explanation given by the hon. member for Vancouver. Then the right hon. gentleman stated in this debate a day or so ago, referring to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's:

I have shown by the tables I have read how an unfair impression may be conveyed by giving the average showing averages by range of duty on dutiable goods.
Let me give another illustration. Take the rate of duty on dutiable goods for the year 1920. The amount of dutiable goods imported in that year was $693,655,165, and the duty collected was $187,524,181.77, or an average on dutiable goods of 27.32 per cent. In his speech a few days ago the right hon. the Prime Minister stated:
The tariff that he (Mr. Fielding) left at that figure in 'the fiscal year that has just passed averages precisely 21.2 per cent.
So, Sir, the tariff in 1920 was 27.32 per cent on dutiable goods, and for the year just closed, according to the figures given by the Prime Minister, 21.2 per cent. One might infer from the argument of the righj: hon. the Prime Minister with regard to fiscal changes under the Liberal regime that the tariff'brought down by the Budget of last year was very much lower than it had been previous to that time; but that is not the case. So the method of argument that was followed by the Prime Minister is not a correct method. It does not show the true comparison with regard to the tariff, and I submit' to the House and the country that the only correct way, if you are going to take averages, is to take the average, of imports and the duty collected thereon.

The average percentage of duty for the .fifteen years under the Liberal rule was 16.29, and the average under the eight years of Conservative rule 17.41. This table is given in page 13 of the report of the Customs Department for the year 19191920. It shows that there was a reduction, under Liberal rule, of 2.41 per cent oi) the whole amount of dutiable and free goods, and that under Conservative rule, from 1911 to 1920, there was an increase of 1.74 per cent. Now, sir, in the face of these figures in the blue book how can the Prime Minister justify the statement that the tariff reduction to-day is forty times greater than it was under Liberal rule. It is absurd. Further than that, the Liberal government in 1911 entered into an agreement know as the reciprocity Pact, by which many more items would have been added to the free list. I find on looking over the returns that during the Liberal rule there were 122 items added to that list and only 18 items added during the Conservative regime. The fact of the matter is that in the campaign of 1911 such a sentiment was aroused in the country that it was impossible for any Government to refuse to add those items to the list which were placed there during the last ten years. A feeling of resentment was displayed by a great many of the people when they found that the reciprocity agreement had been defeated at the polls; and a large percentage of the adverse vote were cast by those who supported the Conservative party at that time. The feeling if disappointment was so strong, and the public sentiment so pronounced, that the Government were obliged to add the items in question to the free list.
In the province from which I come the tariff question is a very live issue. It is not satisfactory to the people of Eastern Canada to hear the Prime Minister and '

the Minister of Finance say that we can afford to wait and see what is to be done in the United States before we undertake tariff revision in this country. That is not a policy that will make for good under the present circumstances. Canada being the smaller country, we cannot afford to pursue a policy of retaliation in regard to the United States tariff. We must, if possible, keep in touch with our good friends in the United States. There is a sentiment in that country, as well as in Canada, that favours a moderate tariff, a lower tariff, a tariff for revenue only rather than a high protective tariff. In support of that statement* let me quote the words whiph were uttered by the late President of the United States when he vetoed the Fordney Bill. On that occasion Mr. Wilson said:
I do not believe that the sober judgment of the masses of the people of the nation, or even of the special class whose interests are immediately; affected by this measure, will sanction a return, especially in view of conditions which lend even less justification for such action, to a policy of legislation for selfish interests which will foster monopoly and increase the disposition to look upon the Government as an instrument for private gain instead of an interest for the promotion of the general well-being'.
He said further:
It 'S obvious that for the commodities, except sugar and wool mentioned in the measure which make up the greater part of our agricultural international trade, the imports can have little or no effect on the prices of the domestic products.
This is strikingly tr,ue of such commodities as wheat and corn. The imports of wheat have come mainly from Canada and Argentina and have not competed with the domestic crop. Rather they have supplemented it.
That expression of sentiment by the President of the United States is supported by a great many people in that country, and if we in Canada adopt a policy of "wait and see," or of retaliation, in response to the tariff that may be imposed by the high protectionists at Washington, we cannot expect to be able to negotiate trade arrangements, as between the two countries, that will be favourable to us. We, as the smaller nation, stand to lose in the event of high tariffs being brought into operation between Canada and the United States. In Eastern Canada a condition exists which is more extreme than has been experienced for many years. In our cellars we have a crop of potatoes that it was impossible to move entirely last fall -our communications with the mainland were not good-and to-day we have two million bushels stored that are not worth
anything. It is quite true that we did not this year enjoy a market in the eastern states. Speaking generally, however, [DOT] and taking the average of one year with another, we have always had a market in the eastern states for our surplus stock of potatoes-potatoes grown in Eastern Canada but not needed there for consumption. We now have facilities for moving these products down the seaboard to the Atlantic ports; and it looks as though we might, in the very near future, have a very cheap method of transportation by water, because rates are coming down every day and competition is becoming keener between the water carriers. It is therefore to our advantage to have an open market in the United States for our products. In view of the contemplated tariff legislation in the United States are we going to make conditions better by resorting to retaliatory measures? No, the results will be much worse for the Canadian consumer and there will be no advantage for the Canadian producer. Because, as I see it, and I think I am correct, the American market of 120 millions of people controls the price as between that country and Canada. The proportionately small amount that we export to the United States makes no difference to the price in that country. On the other hand, if they put up a tariff to keep our products out of the American market and send their low-grade goods, -of which their surplus in food products largely consists-into Canada, they can demoralize the market in this country. That is, as regards low grade goods. In products of the higher standard we can compete with them in the open market because the quality of what we have to sell is equal, if not superior, to theirs. Under favourable conditions we can obtain a market in the United States for our eastern products at a comparatively small expenditure; and the people of Central Canada can trade with their neighbours across the international boundary line much in the same way. But the higher the tariff is made the worse it will be for the people of Eastern Canada, they are the ones than will suffer.
Another product that we are finding an excellent market for in the United States, ever since the duty was removed is eggs. In the last few years the farmers in Eastern Canada have been shipping their fresh eggs to the United States, and have built up a splendid trade with that country. The success achieved in that way has done a good deal to encourage the egg trade.

The farmers have been encouraged to improve the quality of their output and today the quality of the eggs produced in Eastern Canada compares favourably to the eggs produced in any other part of Canada, if indeed it is not superior. On the other hand ten years ago the quality of that product was at an extremely low level. These facts tend to substantiate the statement I make that our people in the East will benefit, and have benefited, by a low tariff with the United States, especially in the matter of food products. And if we pursue a policy of retaliation against their increased tariff, without making any approach to them, we cannot expect any-ing else but a tariff war between the two countries.
I wish also. Sir, to make reference to a local matter that is closely related to the ' last subject, and that is the method of getting our goods to market. I do not wish to bring local issues too much into this debate, but it is necessary from the standpoint of attending to every portion of the country that where grievances exist, whether it be in the east or in the west or in the centre, those grievances should be adjusted, otherwise we cannot expect to keep our country united and present a solid front in the .markets of the world. We have in Prince Edward Island a condition that has accentuated the potato situation as I have described it, and that is the method of transportation to the mainland during the winter months. Last fall our farmers taxed the capacity of the railway to its utmost before the season closed for moving out their potatoes. During the winter months owing to the railway being in a state of transition from the narrow gauge to the broad gauge on which work began some years ago and was later suspended, those farmers were able to get out only a very small percentage of their crop, and when the spring opened up they found themselves with large quantities of potatoes on their hands and a very poor market for them; in fact, the freight rates were so high and the market so unsatisfactory that the returns on their potatoes would not pay for the freight and bags. If we had had our transportation system completed we would not have been in such a bad condition, as our crop would be moving during the whole winter. Therefore I want to impress upon the Government the necessity of putting the transportation system in better shape. I would urge them to complete the work. of broadening the gauge which was undertaken some years ago and stopped during the last two years 
of the war for various reasons, which I am not going to refer to nor complain of now, but it was generally held that it was poor policy to discontinue the work.
It is very expensive to operate the railway in its present condition, and the expenditure necessary to. put the railway facilities in good shape is fully justified. It costs more to operate the system under present conditions on account of having to transfer freight from the narrow gauge to the broad gauge, and vice versa, etc. According to the estimates made by competent engineers and endorsed and passed by the board of mahagement of the Canadian National railways-which estimates are now awaiting endorsation by the Department of Railways and Canals-the work could be completed for $650,000. There is another matter, Sir, to which I should like to refer before 'I close. Coming back to more controversial politics I may say that we have an election pending in one constituency in New Brunswick and in one constituency in Quebec, to take place on the 28th of this month. I see by the Ottawa Citizen of May 13, that one of the members of the Government, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) visited the constituency of York-Sunbury and spoke at McAdam on May 12. On that occasion he is quoted as saying.
There has been no government in power since Confederation whose policies could not be justly criticised and accused of dishonesty, yet even its political enemies will not accuse the present Governmnet of misappropriation of funds during the war.
Now, Sir, I want to draw particular attention to that statement of an hon. minister of this Government in a by-election in the province of New Brunswick. What is the record of the Government during the war? Have any accusations been made? I think, Sir, I can justly say to this House and to the country that the statement made by the Minister of Labour is not borne out by the facts that are on record-on the record of the Committees of this House during the war. I refer to the Public Accounts Committee in 1915, when it was proved that the moneys were misappropriated by the Government for war purposes. It was shown before the Public Accounts Committee that there was lost or squandered of the moneys of this country, on horses, $83,000; on bicycles, $28,000; on shield shovels, $30,000; on binoculars, $3,000; on submarines, $250,000; and a large amount on Oliver equipment. It is surprising, Sir, to see a member of the Government going into the country and appealing for support on such a cry-stating, as appears in the press report, that no accusation has been made against the Government when the records of committees of this House show that hundreds of thousands of dollars were squandered- It is evident, therefore, that references and comparisons made, as I have shown, by the right hon. Prime Minister in the House and by his ministers out of the House are not borne out by the facts when the whole truth is told. Mr. Speaker,

the hour is late and I will not detain the House any further.
